content: The field of physical medicine and rehabilitation has emerged to address the specific needs of severely injured patients who are often discharged with significant disabilities. It is highly desirable to have fully trained specialists in this field available at hospitals that manage such patients. These specialists are particularly important in tertiary care facilities, where they can provide advanced care. However, the global shortage of physical medicine and rehabilitation specialists limits the feasibility of making their presence an essential requirement. These specialists possess expertise in managing severely disabled individuals, including neurogenic bladder management, bowel programs, prevention of pressure ulcers, and monitoring for nosocomial infections. Their skills are considered highly desirable in specialist and tertiary care settings, but their limited availability worldwide prevents this recommendation from being universally essential. Electromyography (EMG) is a valuable tool that complements the work of physical medicine and rehabilitation specialists. It is particularly beneficial in evaluating and treating peripheral nerve injuries. This capability is also considered desirable in specialist and tertiary care facilities. Many injured individuals may never regain their pre-injury functional status. Rehabilitation aims to optimize their ability to function in society. The Disability and Rehabilitation (DAR) department of the World Health Organization (WHO) has been addressing these needs through community-based rehabilitation programs. These efforts involve collaboration across various sectors, including ministries of health and other governmental bodies. The WHO’s Guidelines for Essential Trauma Care recognize the importance of such initiatives, although the focus of these guidelines remains on facility-based trauma care. The WHO, through its Department of Essential Drugs and Medicines Policy (EDM), has developed a model list of essential medicines to address major public health problems. This list includes 325 medicines that are evidence-based, safe, and cost-effective. These medicines should be available at all times within a functioning health system, in adequate amounts, appropriate dosage forms, and at an affordable price. The model list is intended to be adapted at the national level, and currently, 156 countries have their own national essential medicines lists. Most of the medications required for essential trauma care are already included in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines. However, their availability remains incomplete, particularly in rural areas of low-income countries. The Guidelines for Essential Trauma Care highlight critical drugs needed for trauma care, drawing from the model list to promote greater availability of trauma-related essential medicines. These guidelines also specify the levels of the healthcare system at which various medicines should be considered essential for injured patients. The WHO emphasizes that the selection of medicines is only the first step, and their appropriate use is equally critical. Healthcare providers must have sufficient training and skills to administer or prescribe these medicines effectively and safely. Regulations and procurement processes must also ensure the availability of essential medicines, particularly in rural and low-income areas. For example, international controls on narcotic drugs can sometimes hinder access to effective analgesics for trauma patients, who represent one of the largest groups in need of pain relief. Amending regulations to ensure the availability of affordable, effective narcotic-level pain medications is a key element of essential trauma care planning. Diagnostic and monitoring equipment, along with the associated expertise, is critical for managing injured patients. Basic tools such as stethoscopes, blood pressure cuffs, thermometers, and urinary catheters are essential at all levels of the healthcare system. Advanced monitoring techniques, such as central venous pressure (CVP) monitoring and intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring, add value to the care of severely injured patients but are not considered essential due to their high costs. Plain-film radiography is essential at higher-level hospitals and desirable at general practitioner-level facilities. Portable X-ray capabilities are essential at tertiary care hospitals and desirable at other levels. Advanced imaging modalities, such as CT scans, MRI, and angiography, provide significant value but are not deemed essential due to their costs. Basic ultrasound is highly useful for both trauma and non-trauma purposes, particularly in obstetrics, and its availability is desirable at specialist and tertiary hospitals. Laboratory tests such as hemoglobin concentration, hematocrit, and serum glucose measurements are essential at all hospital levels. Gram stains are essential at specialist and tertiary hospitals, while tests for electrolytes, arterial blood gases, and serum lactate are desirable but not essential due to cost constraints. Pediatric length-based tapes, such as Broselow tapes, are inexpensive and desirable for calculating fluid and medication doses for injured children. The maintenance of medical equipment is critical to ensure uninterrupted services. Universal precautions to prevent infection are essential, particularly in trauma care settings where exposure to blood and body fluids is common. Healthcare providers must be adequately trained to use diagnostic and monitoring equipment safely and accurately, and quality assurance mechanisms should be in place to monitor the application of tests and procedures.
